title: Acute postoperative haemorrhage

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science & critical care (postoperative complications)
guidelineVersions: BSH major haemorrhage guideline (10 June 2022; last review 22 July 2025)

related.why: haemorrhagic shock after trauma: response to resuscitation
transfusion reaction and major haemorrhage protocol activation

brief.scenario: You are the surgical SHO. A man deteriorates two hours after laparotomy: pulse 125/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, cool peripheries and increasing blood-stained drain output.
brief.task: Explain your immediate assessment and management. You have 9 minutes. The examiner will give further findings and results when you ask for them.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Postoperative tachycardia with deterioration requires urgent assessment for haemorrhage and other causes, including sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Waiting for the haemoglobin to fall, or for crossmatched blood, before treating.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: ABCDE now, two large-bore lines and call the registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory.

flow: Recognise shock and its likely causes
Activate the major haemorrhage protocol if indicated
Find the source and plan definitive control

grid.label: Recognises possible haemorrhage, keeps the differential open
grid.fail: Puts the tachycardia down to pain, or calls it haemorrhage and considers nothing else.
grid.pass: Assesses urgently for haemorrhage and other causes, including sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications.
grid.high: Ranks haemorrhage first from drain output and cool peripheries, and revises the differential as findings arrive.

grid.label: Identifies physiological deterioration
grid.fail: Takes reassurance from one set of observations or a blood pressure that is not yet very low.
grid.pass: Identifies shock from pulse, blood pressure, perfusion, mental state, urine output and lactate.
grid.high: Uses trends rather than isolated observations; a near-normal blood pressure does not exclude major early bleeding.

grid.label: ABCDE, access and monitoring
grid.fail: Repeats observations and watches a deteriorating patient without starting resuscitation.
grid.pass: Starts ABCDE, gives oxygen, obtains two large-bore IV lines and continuous monitoring.
grid.high: Assesses and resuscitates at the same time and reassesses after each intervention.

grid.label: Urgent bloods and point-of-care tests
grid.fail: Sends a crossmatch only and waits for it before acting.
grid.pass: Sends FBC, coagulation tests with fibrinogen, U&E, group and crossmatch, blood gas and lactate.
grid.high: Monitors blood gas, lactate, temperature and ionised calcium repeatedly during resuscitation.

grid.label: Escalates early
grid.fail: Delays calling seniors until the haemoglobin result returns.
grid.pass: Calls the surgical registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory immediately.
grid.high: Gives a concise structured referral and asks for theatre and consultant to be made aware.

grid.label: Major haemorrhage protocol
grid.fail: Waits for crossmatched blood or a falling haemoglobin before giving blood.
grid.pass: Uses emergency blood/components through the major haemorrhage protocol when indicated, without waiting for crossmatching.
grid.high: Prevents hypothermia and corrects coagulopathy under the protocol, guided by fibrinogen and repeat tests.

grid.label: Interprets the early haemoglobin
grid.fail: Is reassured by a haemoglobin of 108 g/L.
grid.pass: Early Hb may remain relatively preserved and underestimate the severity of bleeding.
grid.high: Treats the physiology and ongoing loss rather than the number, and repeats the measurement during resuscitation.

grid.label: Searches for the bleeding source
grid.fail: Looks at the drain only, or sends an unstable patient to CT before resuscitation and escalation.
grid.pass: Examines the wound, drains and abdomen and considers concealed intra-abdominal bleeding.
grid.high: Leaves the imaging decision to the senior team once the patient is stable enough to travel.

grid.label: Definitive haemorrhage control
grid.fail: Plans to keep observing while the patient continues to bleed.
grid.pass: Recognises continued bleeding needs definitive control, which may mean intervention or return to theatre.
grid.high: States that resuscitation and haemorrhage control proceed together, with theatre prepared in parallel.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The nurse is worried about this man two hours after his laparotomy. What do you think is going on?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He is probably in pain after a big operation. I would give him more analgesia and see.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That is not too bad. I would repeat the observations in an hour.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A crossmatch, and I would wait for the blood to be ready before transfusing.

fail.speaker: candidate

fail.text: I would check the drain and send him for a CT to find out.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would keep observing him closely overnight.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The nurse is worried about this man two hours after his laparotomy. What do you think is going on?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Postoperative tachycardia with deterioration needs urgent assessment for haemorrhage and other causes, including sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications.

pass.text: He is shocked: tachycardic, hypotensive and cool. I would check his mental state, urine output and lactate.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would start ABCDE, give oxygen, put in two large-bore IV lines and put him on continuous monitoring.

pass.text: He is still 92/58 mmHg after your first steps.

pass.text: If he continues to bleed he needs definitive control, which may mean intervention or a return to theatre.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nurse is worried about this man two hours after his laparotomy. What do you think is going on?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Postoperative tachycardia with deterioration requires urgent assessment for haemorrhage and other causes, including sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications. The drain output and cool peripheries make haemorrhage my first concern.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am looking at the trend: his pulse has climbed and his blood pressure is falling. A blood pressure that is not yet very low would not reassure me.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would assess and resuscitate together: ABCDE, oxygen, two large-bore IV lines and monitoring, reassessing after each step.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am concerned that this patient may have significant postoperative haemorrhage, and I would activate the major haemorrhage pathway if clinically indicated.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Call the surgical registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory immediately. Obtain two large-bore IV lines; use emergency blood/components through the major haemorrhage protocol when indicated without waiting for crossmatching. Send fibrinogen with coagulation tests; monitor blood gas, lactate, temperature and ionised calcium, prevent hypothermia and correct coagulopathy under the protocol. Resuscitation and haemorrhage control proceed together.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His haemoglobin is 108 g/L. Does that reassure you?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No. Early Hb may remain relatively preserved and underestimate the severity of bleeding. I am treating his physiology and ongoing loss, and I will repeat it during resuscitation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Can we get a CT first to find the source?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not while he is unstable. I would examine the wound, drains and abdomen for concealed bleeding, and the senior team decides on imaging once he is stable enough to travel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am treating this as suspected significant postoperative haemorrhage: resuscitation is underway, blood is being prepared and the senior surgical team has been urgently alerted.

failures.move: Repeats observations and waits while a tachycardic, cool patient deteriorates.
failures.consequence: Shock progresses unrecognised. This is a critical fail.

failures.move: Waits for crossmatched blood when emergency components are indicated.
Takes reassurance from an Hb of 108 g/L.
failures.consequence: The severity of acute bleeding is underestimated.

failures.move: Sends the unstable patient to CT before resuscitation and escalation.
failures.consequence: The patient deteriorates away from help. This is a critical fail.

recovery.when: If you started with a long history
recovery.line: I need to treat his physiology first. I am starting ABCDE and calling the registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory now.

knowledge.fact: Postoperative tachycardia with deterioration has a differential: haemorrhage, sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications.
Early Hb may remain relatively preserved and underestimate the severity of bleeding.
In major haemorrhage, emergency blood and components are given through the protocol without waiting for crossmatching; fibrinogen is sent with coagulation tests.
Monitor blood gas, lactate, temperature and ionised calcium; prevent hypothermia and correct coagulopathy under the protocol.

recall.think: Bleeding after laparotomy until assessment points elsewhere; keep sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac causes in mind.
recall.say: “I am concerned this is significant postoperative haemorrhage. I need the registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory now.”
do: ABCDE, oxygen, two large-bore IV lines
Bloods with fibrinogen, crossmatch, gas and lactate

numbers.meaning: early Hb may remain relatively preserved; it does not exclude major bleeding

recall.trap: A near-normal haemoglobin or blood pressure.
recall.finish: Definitive haemorrhage control: intervention or return to theatre, in parallel with resuscitation.

sources.name: BSH, Haematological management of major haemorrhage
sources.supports: Major haemorrhage protocol activation, emergency components without waiting for crossmatch, fibrinogen, calcium and temperature monitoring, correction of coagulopathy.

push.question: What are the possible causes of his tachycardia?
push.expect: Haemorrhage first, plus sepsis, hypoxia and cardiac complications.

push.question: Who do you call, and when?
push.expect: Registrar, anaesthetist and transfusion laboratory immediately.

push.question: Would an Hb of 108 g/L reassure you?
push.expect: No: early Hb may remain relatively preserved.

push.question: What is ultimately required if bleeding continues?
push.expect: Definitive haemorrhage control: intervention or return to theatre.

curveballs.prompt: Can we get a CT first to find the source?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not while unstable: resuscitate and escalate first; imaging is a senior decision once he is stable enough.

curveballs.prompt: The crossmatch will take 40 minutes. Shall we wait?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: use emergency blood/components through the major haemorrhage protocol when indicated.
